lexemes.note: Pattern קָטָל (Wiktionary). Mostly used in the plural for the pickled buds.

profile.feeling: Small salty-sour green buds — and a thorny bush growing out of old stone walls.

senses.def: caper — the pickled flower bud of Capparis spinosa, a condiment

examples.tr: She adds capers to the sauce.
Capers are sour and salty.

examples.text: הַצָּלָף צוֹמֵחַ בֵּין הָאֲבָנִים שֶׁל הַכֹּתֶל.
examples.tr: The caper bush grows between the stones of the Western Wall.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this noun (pattern קָטָל). The homograph צַלָּף “sniper” belongs to the verb צָלַף “to whip, to snipe”, which Wiktionary says is possibly the same word.

funFacts: German Kapern, Russian каперсы, Greek κάππαρη and Turkish kapari all go back to Greek κάππαρις; Hebrew has its own word, צָלָף.
The caper bush is one of the plants that grow out of the stones of the Western Wall in Jerusalem.
pitfalls: צָלָף “caper” and צַלָּף “sniper” are both spelled צלף; only the vowels and the context tell them apart.
Count noun: one bud is צָלָף, but the food is nearly always צְלָפִים.
subtleties: Ecclesiastes 12:5 says וְתָפֵר הָאֲבִיּוֹנָה, traditionally understood as “the caper berry shall fail”; אֲבִיּוֹנָה is the caper berry, צָלָף the plant and its bud.
After the article the צ is doubled: הַצָּלָף, הַצְּלָפִים.

lexemes.note: A loanword used as a mass noun. Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry.

profile.feeling: The dark green sheet around a sushi roll; crisp, salty, of the sea.

senses.def: nori — dried edible seaweed (laver, Pyropia) pressed into thin sheets

examples.tr: I (m.) roll sushi in a sheet of nori.
The children eat nori snacks.
Nori is made from seaweed.

synonyms.nuance: “seaweed, alga” in general; at the sushi bar the nori sheet is often simply הָאַצָּה

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. From Japanese 海苔 (nori), like English nori (Wiktionary: the kanji literally mean “ocean moss”, but are only a spelling of the native word, from Proto-Japonic *nǝri).

funFacts: Chinese writes 海苔 hǎitái with the same characters; the dried laver of Chinese soups is 紫菜 zǐcài, “purple vegetable”.
The British phycologist Kathleen Drew-Baker worked out the life cycle of laver in 1949, which rescued Japanese nori farming; she is honoured in Japan as the “Mother of the Sea”.
pitfalls: Masculine and without a plural: count the sheets with דַּף — שְׁנֵי דַּפֵּי נוֹרִי.
subtleties: At the sushi bar people often just say הָאַצָּה (“the seaweed”) for the nori sheet.
Unvocalized נורי has the same letters as the given name Nuri.

lexemes.note: Used as a mass noun. Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. The dagesh in בּ marks b (a loanword); everyday spelling לוביה.

profile.feeling: Long, thin green pods in a tomato stew — and the black-eyed peas of the Rosh Hashanah table.

senses.def: yardlong bean — the long green pods of the cowpea (Vigna unguiculata), eaten as a vegetable
black-eyed peas — the dried seeds of the same plant

examples.tr: Mom cooks yardlong beans with tomatoes.
The yardlong beans at the market are long and thin.

examples.text: בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה אוֹכְלִים לוּבְּיָה לְסִימָן טוֹב.
examples.tr: At Rosh Hashanah people eat black-eyed peas as a good omen.

synonyms.nuance: the general word for beans (Phaseolus); לוּבְּיָה names the cowpea specifically

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. Compare Arabic لُوبِيَا (lūbiyā, “black-eyed peas”), which Wiktionary derives from Classical Persian لوبیا (lōbiyā), Classical Syriac ܠܘܒܝܐ (lōbyā) or directly from Ancient Greek λόβια, plural of λόβιον “pod”.

funFacts: The same word travelled far: Turkish lobya, Georgian ლობიო (lobio) — known to Russian speakers as the bean dish лобио — and Persian lubia, all from Greek λόβιον “pod”.
A single pod can grow to half a metre; English calls it the yardlong bean, Chinese 豇豆 jiāngdòu.
pitfalls: לוּבְּיָה can mean the long green pods or the dried black-eyed peas; the context (or the shop shelf) decides.
subtleties: The dagesh in בּ keeps the sound b; without it the letter would read v.

lexemes.note: A recent loanword used as a mass noun; masculine like other loanwords not ending in -a. Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry.

profile.feeling: A bowl of salted green pods at the start of a sushi meal.

senses.def: edamame — young green soybeans in the pod, boiled or steamed and salted

examples.text: בַּמִּסְעָדָה הַיַּפָּנִית הִזְמַנּוּ אֶדָמָמֶה עִם מֶלַח גַּס.
examples.tr: At the Japanese restaurant we ordered edamame with coarse salt.

examples.text: אֶת הָאֶדָמָמֶה מְבַשְּׁלִים חָמֵשׁ דַּקּוֹת בְּמַיִם רוֹתְחִים.
examples.tr: Edamame is boiled for five minutes in boiling water.

examples.text: אֶדָמָמֶה זֶה סוֹיָה צְעִירָה בְּתוֹךְ הַתַּרְמִיל.
examples.tr: Edamame is young soy in the pod.

synonyms.nuance: “soybeans” in general, also the dry ones; אֶדָמָמֶה are the young green pods

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. From Japanese 枝豆 (edamame), literally “stem beans” (Wiktionary, English entry edamame).

funFacts: Chinese calls the same pods 毛豆 máodòu, “hairy beans”, after the fuzz on the pods.
Edamame are ordinary soybeans picked before they ripen and dry.
pitfalls: It looks like אֲדָמָה “earth, soil” + מֶה — a pure coincidence; the word is Japanese.
The final -e is not the feminine -a: it is treated as masculine, like other such loanwords.
subtleties: Used without a plural, for the dish or the beans.
Only the beans are eaten; the pod is squeezed between the teeth and left.

lexemes.note: Pronounced fakús: the פ has no dagesh (f), also after the article. Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry; its English entry Armenian cucumber gives פקוס (fakús, masculine).

profile.feeling: A long, pale, ribbed “cucumber” of the summer market — crisp and mild.

senses.def: Armenian cucumber, snake melon (Cucumis melo var. flexuosus), eaten raw like a cucumber

examples.tr: In summer people buy Armenian cucumbers at the market.

examples.text: הַפַקּוּס בָּהִיר וְאָרֹךְ יוֹתֵר מִמְּלָפְפוֹן רָגִיל.
examples.tr: The Armenian cucumber is paler and longer than an ordinary cucumber.
Armenian cucumber is crisp and refreshing in a salad.

synonyms.nuance: “Armenian cucumber”, the descriptive name of books and seed catalogues

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. From Arabic فَقُّوس (faqqūs, “Armenian cucumber”), which Wiktionary traces to Aramaic and relates to Aramaic פַּקּוּעָא (paqqūʿā, “a type of gourd”) ; compare the wild gourds, פַּקֻּעֹת שָׂדֶה, of 2 Kings 4:39.

funFacts: Botanically it is a melon (Cucumis melo), not a cucumber — hence names like snake melon.
Some scholars identify the קִשֻּׁאִים that the Israelites missed in Egypt (Numbers 11:5) with this melon-cucumber.
pitfalls: The first letter is f, not p: fakús.
It is not a מְלָפְפוֹן (cucumber) to a botanist, although it is eaten like one.
subtleties: A word of the market, borrowed from Arabic; in books and seed catalogues it is מְלָפְפוֹן אַרְמֶנִי.

profile.feeling: Golden blossoms stuffed with cheese and fried — a summer restaurant treat.

senses.def: zucchini flower, squash blossom (eaten stuffed or fried)

examples.text: בַּמִּסְעָדָה הִזְמַנְתִּי פִּרְחֵי קִשּׁוּא מְמֻלָּאִים בִּגְבִינָה.
examples.tr: At the restaurant I ordered zucchini flowers stuffed with cheese.

examples.text: אֶת פִּרְחֵי הַקִּשּׁוּא קוֹטְפִים בַּבֹּקֶר, כְּשֶׁהֵם פְּתוּחִים.
examples.tr: Zucchini flowers are picked in the morning, when they are open.

examples.text: פֶּרַח קִשּׁוּא מְטֻגָּן הוּא מָנָה אִיטַלְקִית קְלָאסִית.
examples.tr: A fried zucchini flower is a classic Italian dish.

synonyms.nuance: with the Italian/English zucchini; frequent on restaurant menus

etymology.text: פֶּרַח “flower” (Wiktionary: cognate with Arabic فَرْخ, “chick, sprout”, and Aramaic פְּרַח “to fly”) + קִשּׁוּא “zucchini” (Wiktionary: compare Arabic كوسة).

funFacts: Stuffed zucchini flowers are a classic in Greece (κολοκυθοανθοί) and Turkey (kabak çiçeği dolması) as well as in Italy (fiori di zucca).
Mostly the male flowers are picked, so the plant still sets fruit.
pitfalls: The plural changes the first word: פִּרְחֵי קִשּׁוּא (not *פְּרָחִים קִשּׁוּא).
The article goes on the second word: פִּרְחֵי הַקִּשּׁוּא.
subtleties: On menus the Italian word is common too: פִּרְחֵי זוּקִינִי.
Everyday spelling with י: פרחי קישוא.

ref.src: Composed from the Wiktionary (kaikki.org) entries דְּלַעַת (plural דְּלוּעִים) and סְפָּגֶטִי (no entry for the phrase)

profile.feeling: A yellow squash whose baked flesh falls apart into “noodles”.

senses.def: spaghetti squash (Cucurbita pepo), whose cooked flesh separates into strands

examples.tr: I (f.) bake a spaghetti squash in the oven.

examples.text: בְּתוֹךְ דְּלַעַת הַסְּפָּגֶטִי יֵשׁ סִיבִים דַּקִּים כְּמוֹ אִטְרִיּוֹת.
examples.tr: Inside the spaghetti squash there are thin strands like noodles.
They grow spaghetti squashes in the garden.

etymology.text: דְּלַעַת “pumpkin, gourd, squash” (Wiktionary: compare Arabic دَلَّاع, “watermelon”) + סְפָּגֶטִי “spaghetti” (from Italian) — like English spaghetti squash and German Spaghettikürbis.

funFacts: It is the same species as the zucchini (קִשּׁוּא), Cucurbita pepo.
A favourite of low-carb cooking: the strands are served like pasta, with tomato sauce.
pitfalls: The plural changes the first word: דְּלוּעֵי סְפָּגֶטִי.
The article goes on the second word: דְּלַעַת הַסְּפָּגֶטִי.
subtleties: Feminine, after דְּלַעַת: דְּלַעַת סְפָּגֶטִי אֲפוּיָה.
The strands appear only after cooking: the flesh is scraped out with a fork.
